text: Say the city's name and you are speaking a word for an onion.
Chicago is a French spelling of shikaakwa,
a Miami-Illinois word for the wild leek that grew thick in the river bottoms.
In 1687 one of La Salle's men wrote that people called the place Chicagou because
of the quantity of wild garlic in the woods.
The city is named for an onion.
The United States arrived as a garrison.
soldiers under Captain John Whistler built Fort Dearborn at the mouth of the river.
A sandbar shaped like an elephant's trunk blocked the harbor,
so the river bent south and ran parallel to the lake before it found a way out.
Ships anchored offshore and waited.
The garrison never held the ground easily.
In 1812 the soldiers abandoned the fort, Potawatomi fighters attacked the column as it left,
and the place burned, then rebuilt four years later.
For most of three decades that lone fort was nearly all that passed for a town.
The land changed hands on paper first.
the same Three Fires nations signed the Treaty of St. Louis and ceded a strip
about twenty miles wide,
running from the lake to the Illinois River, the exact ground a canal would need.
Surveyors drew it as the Indian Boundary Line.
A few Chicago streets still run that old diagonal today, cutting across the grid,
because they trace a line that predates the grid.
And the men who wanted that canal corridor had only begun.
